text: Kenneth Jinghwa Hsu (simplified Chinese: 许靖华; traditional Chinese: 許靖華; pinyin: Xǔ Jìnghuá), Ph.D., M.A., born on 28 June 1929, is a Chinese scientist, geologist, paleoclimatologist, oceanographer, government advisor, author, inventor, and entrepreneur born in Nanjing, China. He earned a B.Sc. from the Chinese National Central University (later renamed Nanjing University in mainland China and reinstated in Taiwan) in 1948, followed by a M.A. from Ohio State University in 1950 and a Ph.D. from the University of California, Los Angeles in 1953. Hsu worked as a petroleum geologist for the Shell Development Corporation (now Shell Oil Company) in Houston, Texas, from 1954 to 1963, then served as an associate professor at two U.S. universities from 1963 to 1967. He became a professor of geology at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH Zürich) from 1967 to 1994, where he promoted experimental geology and established five leading international laboratories in rock mechanics (geophysics), mass-spectrometry (isotope geochemistry), Quaternary research (paleoclimatology), sedimentology, and tectonics. After retiring in 1994, he transitioned into environmental engineering. During his tenure at ETH Zürich, he was invited as lecturer, guest, or honorary professor in geology, climatology, or oceanography to numerous global institutions, including Beijing, San Diego, Cambridge, Columbia, Florence, Harvard, London, Milan, M.I.T., Moscow, Nanjing, Naples, Ohio, Oxford, Paris, Princeton, Taipei, Tokyo, Toronto, Washington, Woods Hole, and Yale. Post-retirement, he held guest professorships at National Taiwan University (1994–95), senior fellowships at the Berlin Institute of Advanced Studies (1995–96), Keck Professorship at Colorado School of Mines, guest professorship at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and university professorships at Nanjing University and Beijing University of Geosciences. Hsu contributed to the Earth Science Revolution of the 1960s by consolidating Plate Tectonics Theory and championed 'Process Oriented Geology,' aligning with the evolutionary biology of Lynn Margulis, the Gaia hypothesis of James Lovelock, and others, emphasizing physical, chemical, and biological processes in geological problems and advocating educational reform in geology. His research included sedimentation in isostatically driven tectonic basins, active margins of continental plates, physical chemistry of evaporites and pelagic diagenesis, granulite formation, catastrophic effects of meteorite impacts, extinction of life forms, and limnology of Lake Zurich. He participated in and led five deep-sea drilling cruises to the South Atlantic, Mediterranean, and Black Sea, and led international expeditions to Tibet, Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia, South China, California Coast Ranges, and the Swiss Alps, traveling to 80 countries for Earth Science. Hsu received numerous medals and awards. He was elected a Member of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences in 1986, becoming a Foreign Associate due to circumstances, and was also an Associate of the Third-World Academy of Sciences, a Member of Academia Sinica (1988), the Mediterranean Academy of Sciences, and several other academies. He co-founded the European Geophysical Society and the science of paleoceanography, convened the First International Conference of Paleoceanography, founded the journal Paleoceanography, and assisted in founding the Asian Association of Marine Geology. He served 11 years as President of the International Association of Sedimentologists and convened the Third Workshop on Marine Geology of IUGS, the First Earth Science Colloquium of the European Science Foundation, several Dahlem Conferences, and numerous symposia and workshops for IGP, ILP, IGCP, SCOR, and JOIDE. Hsu edited numerous scientific journals and held advisory roles for governments of developing countries. He co-organized a consortium of 15 European member states to join the International Ocean Drilling Program. He successfully lobbied for the Chinese Geological Union to replace the Chinese Geological Society in Taipei as a member of the International Union of Geological Sciences and was part of the first IUGS delegation to China. He provided training programs for Sedimentology (1979), Field Geology of Tibet (1980), and Plate Tectonics (1992) for the Chinese Ministry of Geology and Mining, and from 1983 to 1995, assisted the Institute of Geology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences with a plate tectonics project and the publication of a new Geological Atlas of China. On his 60th and 70th birthdays, colleagues published two Festschrift symposia books: Controversies in Geology and Paradoxes in Geology. In September 2009, his contributions to China and science were recognized in a Beijing conference attended by government, industry, and academic dignitaries. After retirement, Hsu founded companies including Tarim Resource Recycling Limited (UK, 2003), Kenneth Hsu IHC Technology & Development Limited (China, 2005), and Lazarus Energy International Limited (UK, 2007), and held 16 patents in mining, petroleum, water, carbon, energy, and environmental management, including the Hydro-Transistor and Integrated Hydrologic Circuit (IHC). His technologies applied in China included enhanced oil recovery techniques. In 2000, Hsu combined hydro-fracturing, horizontal drilling, and water flooding to invent a new residual oil recovery (ROR) process called 3-dimensional fluid injection, which could increase world recoverable petroleum reserves by 50% or more, using water (or carbon dioxide). With support from Chinese Prime Minister Wen Jiabao, an expert panel convened by former Petroleum Minister Dr. Wang Tao unanimously approved the ROR invention for testing and application in China. In April 2006, PetroChina reported a successful test at the Changqing Oil Field (discovered in 1907), where annual production rose from about 10,000 tons prior to the test to 10 million tons in 2006 and 20 million tons in 2007. Hsu is active in institutions and organizations to apply new technologies in China and internationally, serving as president of the IHC Technology & Development Corporation (China), senior advisor and chief engineer at the Kenneth Hsu Institute for IHC Development (National Institute of Earth Sciences, Beijing), and director of the Center for Environmental & Health Engineering (Henan University, Kaifeng). His work on nitrite in drinking water and cancer was documented in The Ecologist journal. Hsu authored or edited over 20 books in multiple languages and was elected International Writer of the Year by the International Book Club (Cambridge, UK) in 2003. His books include The Mediterranean Was A Desert (1982), which detailed the Messinian Salinity Crisis and the 1970 D/V Glomar Challenger Leg 13 expedition, leading to the hypothesis that the Mediterranean was a desert 5.5 million years ago; the book was selected by Philip Morrison of Scientific American as one of the 100 most significant and influential science books of the 20th century and was adapted into a PBS film. Challenger At Sea (1983) served as an overview of marine geology and a textbook for non-majors. The Great Dying (1986) described the cometary impact theory behind the dinosaur extinction, sold over 170,000 copies worldwide, and reached 28,000 in the U.S. and 100,000 in mainland China in 1989, with 40,000 in Taiwan; it was featured in Taipei’s United Post best-seller list for over a year and named a top non-fiction book of the year in August 1992. The book challenged Charles Darwin’s theory of natural selection, arguing that most extinctions are caused by catastrophes and that evolution is governed by chance rather than gradual improvement, endorsing catastrophism and non-Darwinian evolution. Klima Macht Geschichte (2000) proposed a theory linking climate and history, predicting global cooling and a little ice age before 2500, supported by scientists including Khabibullo Abdusamatov, Yuk Yung, John Cassey, Nigel Calder, Henrik Svensmark, Alexander Chizhevsky, and John D. Hamaker; it was based on Hsu’s earlier paper 'Is Gaia Endothermic?' and referenced in a 1992 Geographical Magazine article. Amadeus & Magdalena (2002), published in Chinese, English, and German with a Chinese title "莫扎特的愛與死," presented Hsu’s musicological theory on the death of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. Hsu has authored or co-authored more than 400 scientific articles across diverse fields including Archaeology, Cancer, Chronon Physics, Climatology, Cosmology, Cytology, Epistemology, Evolution, Fractal Geometry, Gaia, Geology, Heliobiology, History, Hydro-Physics, Languages, Marine Biology, Mathematics, Music, Oceanography, Palaeontology, Paleoclimatology, Philosophy, Politics, Religion, and Symbiogenesis.
